subject: Science
title: Priya's Garden Mystery
hook: Help Priya discover the secret parts of plants and how they grow.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: curious student who tends her grandmother's garden

characters.name: Dadi
characters.role: grandmother who knows all about plants

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Priya's friend who helps dig and observe

slides.title: Plants in Detail
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun dig up a tomato plant from Dadi's garden to see what's hidden underground.

image.alt: Plants in Detail — Plants in Detail

slides.title: Dadi's Garden Discovery
slides.storyContext: On a Saturday morning, Priya finds a healthy tomato plant with bright red fruits. She asks Dadi: 'How does the plant make tomatoes?' Dadi smiles and says: 'Let's dig carefully and see all the parts that help the plant grow and feed itself.'

image.alt: Dadi's Garden Discovery — Plants in Detail

slides.title: Roots - The Underground Workers
slides.storyContext: Arjun digs around the plant and finds long, thin, white threads going deep into the soil.

points.label: What roots do
points.text: Roots hold the plant firmly in soil and suck up water and nutrients from the ground.

points.label: Root types
points.text: Fibrous roots (like grass) are thin and spread out. Tap roots (like radish) go straight down.

example.problem: Why does a tomato plant not fall over in wind?
example.solution: Strong roots grip the soil tightly, acting like an anchor.

slides.inSimpleWords: Roots are like tiny drinking straws buried in soil — they take in water and minerals that help the plant grow.

image.alt: Roots - The Underground Workers — Plants in Detail

slides.title: Stem - The Plant's Backbone
slides.storyContext: Priya touches the thick green stem and traces it from soil to the leaves and flowers.

points.label: Main job
points.text: The stem holds up leaves and flowers toward sunlight and carries water from roots to leaves.

points.label: Stem types
points.text: Green herbaceous stems (like tomato) are soft. Woody stems (like neem tree) are hard and brown.

example.problem: If you cut a tomato plant's stem, does it still get water?
example.solution: No — the water comes from roots through the stem. A broken stem stops the flow.

slides.inSimpleWords: The stem is a highway carrying water upward and holding the plant upright like a skeleton.

image.alt: Stem - The Plant's Backbone — Plants in Detail

slides.title: Leaves - The Food Makers
slides.storyContext: Priya holds a green tomato leaf up to the sun and notices tiny veins running through it.

points.label: Photosynthesis
points.text: Leaves use sunlight, water, and air to make their own food (glucose). This is photosynthesis.

points.label: Leaf parts
points.text: Blade (flat green part), veins (carry water and food), petiole (stem connecting to plant).

example.problem: Why are leaves green?
example.solution: Leaves contain a green pigment called chlorophyll that captures sunlight to make food.

slides.inSimpleWords: Leaves are tiny food factories — they trap sunlight and turn it into energy for the whole plant.

image.alt: Leaves - The Food Makers — Plants in Detail

slides.title: Flowers - Making Seeds
slides.storyContext: Dadi shows Priya a bright yellow tomato flower before the tomato grows.

points.label: Flower parts
points.text: Sepal (green outer), petal (colorful), stamen (male, makes pollen), pistil (female, makes seeds).

points.label: Pollination
points.text: Bees or wind carry pollen from stamen to pistil. This helps make seeds.

example.problem: Why do flowers have bright colors and sweet smells?
example.solution: To attract bees and insects that carry pollen from one flower to another.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flowers are where seeds are born — they need pollen from another flower to start the process.

image.alt: Flowers - Making Seeds — Plants in Detail

slides.title: Fruits and Seeds
slides.storyContext: The yellow flower turns into a green, then red tomato. Priya cuts it open and sees many seeds inside.

points.label: Fruit
points.text: The ripe fruit protects seeds. It's sweet and attracts animals to spread seeds far away.

points.label: Seeds
points.text: Each seed has a baby plant (embryo), stored food, and a seed coat for protection.

example.problem: Why are mango fruits sweet and juicy?
example.solution: The sweet fruit attracts birds to eat it and drop seeds far from the tree — nature's delivery system.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fruits and seeds are the plant's way of making babies and spreading them across the world.

image.alt: Fruits and Seeds — Plants in Detail

slides.title: How a Bean Seed Grows
slides.storyContext: Arjun planted a bean seed in Dadi's garden two weeks ago. Now Priya watches it sprout.

example.problem: A bean seed needs water, air, and warmth to sprout. What happens first?
example.solution: Water softens the seed coat. The root breaks out first (goes down), then the shoot pushes up with baby leaves. The stored food in the seed feeds the baby plant until leaves can make their own food.

slides.inSimpleWords: Seeds are sleeping babies waiting for water and warmth to wake up and grow.

image.alt: How a Bean Seed Grows — Plants in Detail

slides.title: Can You Spot the Plant Parts?
slides.storyContext: Dadi gives Priya a drawing of a neem tree and asks: identify all the parts and tell what each one does.

example.problem: Look at a tree. Which part soaks up water? Which part makes food? Which part holds seeds?
example.solution: Roots soak up water. Leaves make food using sunlight. Fruits hold seeds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every plant part has a job — roots drink, stems carry, leaves eat, flowers make babies, fruits protect seeds.

image.alt: Can You Spot the Plant Parts? — Plants in Detail

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun now know plants are like tiny communities with special jobs for each part.

points.text: Roots anchor the plant and drink water with minerals from soil.
Stems carry water and hold the plant upright.
Leaves use sunlight to make food (photosynthesis).
Flowers attract insects with pollen to make seeds.
Fruits protect seeds and help them spread to new places.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants are amazing — each part does a special job so the plant can grow, make food, and create new plants.

image.alt: What We Learned — Plants in Detail

subject: Science
title: Rahul's Wildlife Adventure
hook: Journey with Rahul to see how animals adapt to their homes — desert, jungle, water, and sky.

characters.name: Rahul
characters.role: curious about why animals look and behave differently

characters.name: Wildlife Guide Sharma
characters.role: expert who teaches about animal adaptations

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: Rahul's cousin who asks clever questions

slides.title: Animals - Habitats and Adaptation
slides.storyContext: Rahul visits a wildlife sanctuary and asks: 'Why do lions have manes but tigers have stripes? Why do fish have fins?'

image.alt: Animals - Habitats and Adaptation — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

slides.title: A World of Different Animals
slides.storyContext: On a school field trip to a nature reserve, Rahul sees lions on the grassland, crocodiles in water, eagles in the sky, and scorpions under rocks. Guide Sharma says: 'Every animal is perfectly built for where it lives. Let's discover why.'

image.alt: A World of Different Animals — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

slides.title: What is Habitat?
slides.storyContext: Meera points to different animals in different places and asks: 'Do all animals live in the same place?'

points.label: Habitat
points.text: A habitat is the natural home of an animal — the place where it finds food, water, shelter, and safety.

points.label: Habitat types
points.text: Desert (hot, dry), forest (trees, moisture), grassland (open, windy), water (river, pond, ocean), sky (air).

example.problem: Would a polar bear survive in a desert?
example.solution: No — a polar bear needs ice and cold. A desert has no ice and is extremely hot. The bear cannot find the seals it eats.

slides.inSimpleWords: Habitat is an animal's address — the exact place on Earth where it is happiest and can survive.

image.alt: What is Habitat? — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

slides.title: Desert Adaptations - Heat and Thirst
slides.storyContext: Guide Sharma points to a camel resting in the sand. Rahul asks: 'How does it live without water for so long?'

points.label: Camel adaptations
points.text: Humps store fat (not water, as many think). Thick fur reflects heat. Wide feet don't sink in sand. Can drink 100 liters at once.

points.label: Other desert animals
points.text: Scorpions are nocturnal (active at night to avoid heat). Lizards burrow underground. Desert plants have thorns, not leaves.

example.problem: Why do scorpions come out only at night in a desert?
example.solution: During the day, sand is too hot (50+°C). Scorpions hide underground where it's cooler and wait for night.

slides.inSimpleWords: Desert animals have special bodies — thick fur, big feet, or night habits — to survive heat and find water.

image.alt: Desert Adaptations - Heat and Thirst — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

slides.title: Forest Adaptations - Hide and Hunt
slides.storyContext: In the jungle part of the sanctuary, Meera spots a tiger with orange and black stripes hidden among trees.

points.label: Camouflage
points.text: Tiger stripes blend with shadows and tree trunks — predators hide from prey, prey hides from danger.

points.label: Sharp senses
points.text: Jungle animals have sharp eyes, ears, and noses to find food and sense danger in thick darkness.

points.label: Climbing and swinging
points.text: Monkeys have long arms and tails for balance. Birds have strong feet for gripping branches.

example.problem: Why do snakes in a forest have green skin?
example.solution: Green color makes them invisible among green leaves — they hide from predators and from their prey.

slides.inSimpleWords: Forest animals are dressed and built to hide, hunt, and move silently through thick trees.

image.alt: Forest Adaptations - Hide and Hunt — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

slides.title: Water Adaptations - Swimming and Diving
slides.storyContext: At the sanctuary pond, Rahul watches a crocodile glide silently and a duck waddle on webbed feet.

points.label: Fish adaptations
points.text: Streamlined body for speed. Fins for steering. Gills to breathe underwater. Scales for protection and smooth movement.

points.label: Aquatic animal adaptations
points.text: Ducks have webbed feet for paddling. Crocodiles have eyes, ears, and nostrils on top of head to see without showing body.

points.label: Breathing
points.text: Fish extract oxygen from water using gills. Whales and dolphins breathe air but are born and live in water.

example.problem: Why do fish have scales and fins but ducks have feathers and webbed feet?
example.solution: Fish live their entire life in water so they need scales and fins. Ducks live both on land and water so they need feathers (waterproof and warm) and webbed feet (paddle-like).

slides.inSimpleWords: Water animals have flat bodies, fins, webbed feet, or special breathing to swim, dive, and live underwater.

image.alt: Water Adaptations - Swimming and Diving — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

slides.title: Grassland Adaptations - Running and Speed
slides.storyContext: On the grassland, Rahul watches zebras and gazelles running fast from a distance predator.

points.label: Speed and stamina
points.text: Grazing animals (zebra, deer) have long, powerful legs for running fast away from predators over open ground.

points.label: Eyes and ears
points.text: Eyes on the sides of the head to see danger coming from any direction. Big ears to hear sounds far away.

points.label: Color patterns
points.text: Stripes on zebras confuse predators. Tan color on gazelles blends with dry grass.

example.problem: A gazelle can run 80 km/h. Why does it run so fast?
example.solution: Lions chase from up to 50 km/h. The gazelle must be faster to escape. Its light body and long legs give it the speed advantage.

slides.inSimpleWords: Grassland animals are built for speed — long legs, strong hearts, and super senses to escape danger in open spaces.

image.alt: Grassland Adaptations - Running and Speed — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

slides.title: Sky Adaptations - Flying and Vision
slides.storyContext: An eagle circles overhead with wings spread wide. Meera asks: 'How can it spot an animal from so high up?'

points.label: Wings and feathers
points.text: Hollow bones are light. Large wings and feathers catch air currents for soaring high and far.

points.label: Super vision
points.text: Eagles see 4 times better than humans — can spot a rabbit from 5 km away while flying high.

points.label: Talons and beaks
points.text: Sharp curved talons for gripping prey. Curved beak for tearing food.

example.problem: Why do flying birds have hollow bones?
example.solution: Hollow bones are strong but very light — this helps the bird fly without carrying heavy weight.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flying animals are super light with strong wings and amazing eyes to see prey while soaring in the sky.

image.alt: Sky Adaptations - Flying and Vision — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

slides.title: How the Frog Adapts
slides.storyContext: At the pond, Rahul finds a green frog sitting on a lily pad, half in water, half out.

example.problem: A frog lives on land and in water. What body parts help it?
example.solution: Webbed feet to kick and swim. Moist skin to absorb oxygen. Bulging eyes on top of head to see above water while underwater. Long sticky tongue to catch flying insects on land.

slides.inSimpleWords: The frog is a shape-shifter — it has adapted body parts to live happily both on land and in water.

image.alt: How the Frog Adapts — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

slides.title: Match the Adaptation to the Habitat
slides.storyContext: Guide Sharma gives Rahul a puzzle: a camel, a fish, a penguin, and an eagle. Where does each live and why?

example.problem: Why does a penguin have flippers, thick fur, and swim fast?
example.solution: Penguins live in ice-cold Antarctic water. Flippers help them swim fast to catch fish. Thick fur and blubber (fat) keep them warm in freezing water.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every animal's body is a perfect fit for where it lives — hot desert, cold water, dark forest, or open sky.

image.alt: Match the Adaptation to the Habitat — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

slides.title: Adaptations Connect Animals to Homes
slides.storyContext: Rahul now understands why animals look and act so differently — each is perfectly designed for its habitat.

points.text: Habitat is the natural home where an animal finds food, water, and shelter.
Desert animals are built for heat and thirst — camels, scorpions, lizards.
Forest animals hide, hunt silently, and climb — tigers, monkeys, snakes.
Water animals swim and breathe underwater or hold their breath — fish, ducks, whales.
Grassland animals run fast and see far — zebras, gazelles, deer.
Sky animals are light, have big wings, and see super well — eagles, owls.

slides.inSimpleWords: Adaptation is nature's genius — every animal is a masterpiece built to thrive exactly where it lives.

image.alt: Adaptations Connect Animals to Homes — Animals - Habitats and Adaptation

subject: Science
title: Ananya's Kitchen Discovery
hook: Learn how food feeds your body, from the farmers' field to your plate, in Ananya's village kitchen.

characters.name: Ananya
characters.role: curious about what makes a healthy meal

characters.name: Farmer Uncle
characters.role: grows vegetables and grains in the village

slides.title: Food and Nutrition
slides.storyContext: Ananya helps her mother cook lunch and asks: 'Which foods make me strong? Which give me energy?'

image.alt: Food and Nutrition — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: From Farm to Plate
slides.storyContext: Ananya's mother brings fresh vegetables, rice, and lentils from the market. Farmer Uncle visits and tells her: 'These foods come from my field. Each part of what you eat helps your body in different ways. Let me show you.'

image.alt: From Farm to Plate — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: What is Nutrition?
slides.storyContext: Mummy explains while chopping vegetables: 'Nutrition is how food helps your body grow, work, and stay healthy.'

points.label: Why we eat
points.text: Food gives us energy to run and play. Food helps our bones grow. Food repairs our muscles. Food keeps us from getting sick.

points.label: Nutrients
points.text: Carbohydrates (energy), proteins (strength), fats (warmth and stored energy), vitamins (health), minerals (bones and teeth), water (every cell).

example.problem: Why do you feel tired if you skip breakfast?
example.solution: Breakfast gives carbohydrates (rice, bread) that break down into glucose (sugar) — your body's main fuel. Without breakfast, your energy tank is empty.

slides.inSimpleWords: Nutrition means eating the right mix of foods so your body can grow tall, stay strong, and never get sick.

image.alt: What is Nutrition? — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: Carbohydrates - Energy Food
slides.storyContext: Ananya watches Mummy cook rice and make rotis. 'Mummy, why do you cook grain foods every day?'

points.label: What they do
points.text: Carbohydrates break down into glucose in your stomach. Glucose is fuel for your brain and muscles — it gives you energy to think, run, and play.

points.label: Carbohydrate sources
points.text: Rice, wheat, bread, potatoes, sugar, fruits. They come mostly from plants.

points.label: Quick vs. slow energy
points.text: Sugary foods (candy, jam) give quick energy but make you crash. Whole grains (brown rice, oats) give steady energy all day.

example.problem: A runner eats pasta (carbohydrate) before a race, not chicken (protein). Why?
example.solution: Carbohydrates break down fast into glucose — the fuel the runner's muscles need instantly. Proteins take longer to digest and are used for building, not quick energy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Carbohydrates are your body's gasoline — they burn quickly to power your brain, heart, and legs.

image.alt: Carbohydrates - Energy Food — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: Proteins - Building and Repair
slides.storyContext: Farmer Uncle explains: 'I grow dal (lentils) and grow chickens for eggs. Both have protein to build strong bodies.'

points.label: What proteins do
points.text: Proteins build muscle, bone, hair, and skin. They repair cuts and bruises. They fight germs. They are the building blocks of your body.

points.label: Protein sources
points.text: Eggs, milk, yogurt, cheese, chicken, fish, meat, beans, lentils, peanuts, soy.

points.label: How much you need
points.text: Growing children (like you) need protein every day — at least at two meals — because your body is getting bigger and stronger.

example.problem: Why do mothers tell children to drink milk and eat eggs?
example.solution: Milk and eggs have lots of protein to build strong muscles. They also have calcium for growing bones and teeth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Proteins are builders — they create strong muscles, bones, and skin, and fix damage when you get hurt.

image.alt: Proteins - Building and Repair — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: Fats - Energy and Warmth
slides.storyContext: Mummy heats oil in a pan and explains: 'A little bit of fat keeps you warm and stores energy inside your body.'

points.label: What fats do
points.text: Fats store lots of energy (more than carbohydrates). They keep you warm. They help your brain and skin stay healthy.

points.label: Healthy fats
points.text: Olive oil, peanut oil, ghee, coconut oil, nuts, fish oil, butter (in small amounts).

points.label: Balance matters
points.text: Some fat is needed and good. Too much fat makes you overweight and tired. The right amount gives slow, lasting energy.

example.problem: Why do we need fat but not too much?
example.solution: A little fat keeps organs warm and stores energy for long activities. Too much fat clogs arteries and makes the heart work too hard.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fats are long-burning fuel — your body stores them for energy during times of scarcity and to keep you warm.

image.alt: Fats - Energy and Warmth — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: Vitamins and Minerals - Health Guards
slides.storyContext: Ananya's mother piles colorful vegetables on a plate: orange carrots, green spinach, red tomatoes, yellow papaya. 'Each color brings different vitamins.'

points.label: Vitamins
points.text: Vitamin A (carrots, spinach) helps eyes see. Vitamin C (citrus, tomatoes) helps wounds heal and fights germs. Vitamin D (eggs, milk, sunlight) helps bones grow.

points.label: Minerals
points.text: Calcium (milk, yogurt, greens) builds strong bones and teeth. Iron (spinach, meat) makes blood carry oxygen. Iodine (salt) helps the brain.

points.label: Rainbow eating
points.text: Different colors = different nutrients. Eat red, orange, yellow, green, and purple foods every day to get all vitamins and minerals.

example.problem: Why does a child's teeth fall out and grow back, but an adult's don't?
example.solution: Children are still building bones and teeth, so they need lots of calcium and vitamin D. Adults' bones and teeth are done growing, so they need less.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vitamins and minerals are tiny bodyguards — they keep your eyes sharp, bones strong, blood healthy, and skin glowing.

image.alt: Vitamins and Minerals - Health Guards — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: Water - The Most Important
slides.storyContext: Mummy serves a glass of water to Ananya and says: 'Drink plenty. Your body is 70% water. It needs water to work.'

points.label: What water does
points.text: Water carries nutrients to every cell. It helps digest food. It cools you when you sweat. It carries waste out of your body.

points.label: How much to drink
points.text: Drink 6-8 glasses of plain water every day. More if you exercise or play sports. More if it's hot outside.

points.label: Water sources
points.text: Plain water, milk, juice, soup, and watery fruits (watermelon, orange) all count. Soda and sugary drinks are not healthy water.

example.problem: Why do athletes drink a lot of water during play?
example.solution: When you exercise, your body heats up and sweats to cool down. Sweat is water leaving your body. You must drink water to replace it or you dehydrate.

slides.inSimpleWords: Water is life — it flows through every part of your body to keep everything working smoothly and cool.

image.alt: Water - The Most Important — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: A Balanced Plate
slides.storyContext: Mummy teaches Ananya to plan a healthy lunch: rice (carb), dal (protein), vegetables (vitamins), yogurt (protein and calcium), and water.

example.problem: Design a healthy lunch for a 10-year-old growing child.
example.solution: 1 cup rice or roti (carbohydrate for energy), 1 cup dal or chicken curry (protein for muscles), 2 bowls mixed vegetables (vitamins, minerals), 1 bowl yogurt (protein, calcium), 1 glass water. This gives all six nutrients in the right amounts.

slides.inSimpleWords: A healthy meal has a mix — grains for energy, protein to grow, colorful veggies for health, and water to keep everything flowing.

image.alt: A Balanced Plate — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: Build Your Perfect Day of Eating
slides.storyContext: Ananya must plan breakfast, lunch, snack, and dinner using the nutrition rules she learned.

example.problem: You have 1 hour to play cricket. What should you eat before to have energy but not feel sick?
example.solution: A banana (carbs, easy to digest) or toast with jam (quick carbs) 30 minutes before. After play, eat protein like milk or paneer to repair muscles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eating right at the right time gives your body the energy to play, learn, and grow without crashes or sickness.

image.alt: Build Your Perfect Day of Eating — Food and Nutrition

slides.title: Your Body is What You Eat
slides.storyContext: Ananya now knows that every bite is a choice to help her body grow strong, smart, and healthy.

points.text: Carbohydrates give quick energy to run, play, and think.
Proteins build muscles, bones, hair, and repair your body.
Fats give long-lasting energy and keep you warm.
Vitamins and minerals keep your eyes, bones, blood, and skin healthy.
Water is in every cell and makes everything work.
A balanced meal has all nutrients — eat the rainbow, stay strong.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good nutrition is a superpower — eat well, and your body grows tall, strong, smart, and never gets tired.

image.alt: Your Body is What You Eat — Food and Nutrition

subject: Science
title: Karthik's Matter Lab
hook: Explore solids, liquids, and gases with Karthik as he plays with everyday items and discovers their secrets.

characters.name: Karthik
characters.role: curious scientist who questions everything around him

characters.name: Sister Neha
characters.role: asks unexpected questions that reveal deeper truths

slides.title: Materials, Solids, Liquids, Gases
slides.storyContext: Karthik wonders: 'Why is a rock hard but water is wet? Why can't I see air but I can feel wind?'

slides.title: Everything is Made of Matter
slides.storyContext: Karthik's Science Teacher Priya sets up a simple lab at school with a rock, a glass of water, an air pump, and a balloon. 'Everything around you is made of matter,' she says. 'Let's see why solids, liquids, and gases behave so differently.'

slides.title: What is Matter?
slides.storyContext: Teacher Priya holds up a brick, a cup of water, and an empty balloon. 'All three are matter — everything that has mass and takes up space.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Matter is anything that has mass (weighs something) and volume (takes up space). Every object, liquid, and gas is matter.

points.label: Three states
points.text: Solid (keeps shape), liquid (flows but keeps volume), gas (spreads to fill any space).

points.label: Why they differ
points.text: The difference is how tightly the tiny bits (atoms and molecules) are packed together.

example.problem: Is air matter if you cannot see it?
example.solution: Yes — air has mass (a balloon full of air weighs more than an empty balloon). Air takes up space (it fills the balloon). So air is matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Matter is anything you can feel, see, or weigh — rocks, water, air, paper, food — everything around you.

slides.title: Solids - Fixed Shape and Size
slides.storyContext: Karthik picks up a pencil, a book, a coin, and a wooden block. Sister Neha asks: 'What's the same about all these?'

points.label: What solids are
points.text: Solids have a fixed shape that doesn't change. They have a fixed volume — they don't shrink or grow. You can hold them.

points.label: Why solids are solid
points.text: The atoms and molecules in a solid are packed very tightly together, all holding hands in a rigid grid. They vibrate but stay in place.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Rock, wood, metal, plastic, bone, paper, ice, glass, cement.

example.problem: If you cut a wooden block in half, does it still behave like a solid?
example.solution: Yes — each half keeps its shape and volume. A solid's atoms are bound so tightly that breaking it doesn't change its state of matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Solids are stubborn — they keep their shape and refuse to change, no matter how you move them around.

slides.title: Liquids - Flows but Keeps Volume
slides.storyContext: Teacher Priya pours water into a tall glass, then pours the same water into a wide, flat plate. Karthik notices: 'The water changes shape!'

points.label: What liquids are
points.text: Liquids have no fixed shape — they flow and take the shape of their container. They have a fixed volume — you can measure 1 liter and it stays 1 liter.

points.label: Why liquids flow
points.text: The atoms and molecules in a liquid are loosely packed. They can slide past each other, so the liquid flows and changes shape.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Water, milk, oil, juice, honey, mercury (liquid metal), blood, petrol.

example.problem: You pour 1 liter of water into a tall thin glass, then into a short wide bowl. Has the volume changed?
example.solution: No — it's still 1 liter. The shape changed but the amount of water stayed the same. This is what makes liquids special.

slides.inSimpleWords: Liquids are flexible — they pour and change shape, but the total amount never changes.

image.alt: Liquids - Flows but Keeps Volume — Materials, Solids, Liquids, Gases

slides.title: Gases - Fill Any Space
slides.storyContext: Karthik blows air into a balloon. The balloon expands and gets bigger. 'Where does all the air come from? The air is invisible!'

points.label: What gases are
points.text: Gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume — they spread to fill any space they're in. A gas in a tiny bottle spreads to fill a huge room.

points.label: Why gases spread
points.text: The atoms and molecules in a gas are very far apart and move super fast. They bump into walls and each other, spreading everywhere.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Air, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, water vapor (steam), smoke, helium (balloons), natural gas, chlorine.

example.problem: You open a bottle of perfume in a room. Soon everyone smells it. Why?
example.solution: Perfume liquid evaporates into perfume gas. The gas molecules spread out, bump into air molecules, and travel through the entire room in minutes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gases are free spirits — they zoom around and spread to fill any space, no matter how big or small.

slides.title: Changing Between States
slides.storyContext: Teacher Priya heats ice water over a burner. Karthik watches ice melt to water, then water boil into steam (gas). 'It's still the same stuff!'

points.label: Melting
points.text: Heating a solid breaks some bonds — atoms get loose and slide around. Ice (solid) melts to water (liquid) at 0°C.

points.label: Evaporation
points.text: Heating a liquid gives atoms so much energy they break free. Water (liquid) evaporates to steam/vapor (gas) at 100°C.

points.label: Condensation and freezing
points.text: Cooling reverses it: steam condenses to water, water freezes to ice. Same matter, different state.

example.problem: Ice, water, and steam are all H2O. Why do they behave so differently?
example.solution: The amount of heat energy changes how tightly atoms hold together. Cold = tight grip (ice). Warm = loose slide (water). Hot = zooming free (steam).

slides.inSimpleWords: Heat is magic — it gives atoms energy to break free. Add heat, atoms spread apart (melting and evaporation). Remove heat, they huddle together (freezing and condensation).

slides.title: Properties of Matter
slides.storyContext: Karthik and Neha test different materials: wood, metal, plastic, glass, water, air. They measure hardness, weight, flexibility, and transparency.

points.label: Physical properties
points.text: Shape, size, color, hardness, flexibility, density (heavy or light), solubility (dissolves in water), transparency (see-through).

points.label: Density
points.text: How much mass fits in a certain volume. Lead is dense (heavy and small). Foam is light (lots of space, little mass).

points.label: Solubility
points.text: Some solids dissolve in water (sugar, salt). Some don't (sand, stone). Gases dissolve too (oxygen, CO2).

example.problem: Sugar dissolves in water to become invisible. Is it still matter?
example.solution: Yes — the sugar atoms are still there, mixed between water molecules. You can taste them and heat the water to evaporate it and get the sugar back.

slides.inSimpleWords: Properties are the fingerprints of matter — color, hardness, weight, how it dissolves, what it looks like.

image.alt: Properties of Matter — Materials, Solids, Liquids, Gases

slides.title: Everyday Matter Changes
slides.storyContext: Teacher Priya lists things Karthik sees every day and asks him to identify the state changes.

example.problem: What state changes happen when you cook rice?
example.solution: Solid rice grains → water boils (liquid to gas) → steam rises → rice absorbs liquid water → rice becomes softer but still mostly solid. Multiple changes in one process.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cooking, laundry, weather, and breathing all involve matter changing states — melting, evaporating, freezing, condensing.

slides.title: Sort the Matter Mystery Box
slides.storyContext: Sister Neha puts items in a box: a stone, honey, air, milk, ice, sugar, smoke, oil. Karthik must sort them by state and explain each choice.

example.problem: Air is invisible. How do you know it's a gas and not nothing?
example.solution: Air has mass (a balloon filled with air weighs more than empty). Air takes up space (it fills the balloon and pushes the balloon walls outward). Therefore, air is matter in the gas state.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every material fits into one of three states based on whether it has fixed shape, fixed volume, and how it flows or spreads.

image.alt: Sort the Matter Mystery Box — Materials, Solids, Liquids, Gases

slides.title: Three States, One Matter
slides.storyContext: Karthik now sees that matter is everywhere — rocks, water, air — and each behaves according to its state.

points.text: Matter is anything with mass and volume — everything around you.
Solids keep a fixed shape and volume — atoms are packed tightly.
Liquids flow and take container shape but keep volume — atoms can slide.
Gases spread to fill any space — atoms zoom around freely.
Heat energy changes states: melting, evaporation, condensation, freezing.
Every material has properties: color, hardness, density, whether it dissolves.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ice, water, and steam are the same matter in three forms — temperature is the magician that changes them.

image.alt: Three States, One Matter — Materials, Solids, Liquids, Gases

subject: Science
title: Divya's Sky Diary
hook: Follow Divya as she explores rain, wind, clouds, and seasons — and learns why weather changes.

characters.name: Divya
characters.role: observes clouds and rain in her village

characters.name: Grandpa Hari
characters.role: a farmer who reads the sky and seasons

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Divya's friend who records weather daily

slides.title: Weather and Climate
slides.storyContext: Divya watches dark clouds gather in the sky. 'Grandpa, why does the sky change? When will it rain?'

slides.title: Reading the Sky
slides.storyContext: On a hot afternoon in June, Divya sits with Grandpa Hari in their village field. He points at the western horizon where dark clouds are building. 'Every year the monsoon rains come,' he says. 'The sun heats the ocean, water rises, and the clouds release rain. Let me teach you how this works.'

slides.title: What is Weather?
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Divya note the temperature, clouds, wind, and rain in their notebook every morning for a week.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Weather is the condition of the air right now — hot, cold, rainy, windy, cloudy. Weather changes day to day.

points.label: Weather elements
points.text: Temperature (hot or cold), humidity (wetness in air), wind (moving air), rain, sunshine, clouds.

points.label: Climate
points.text: Climate is the average weather of a place over many years. India's climate is tropical (hot and rainy in monsoon, hot in summer, cool in winter).

example.problem: Today it rained and tomorrow it will be sunny. Is the climate changing?
example.solution: No — weather changed from rainy to sunny. Climate changes only over decades, not days. Climate is the pattern; weather is today's surprise.

slides.inSimpleWords: Weather is what happens today. Climate is the pattern of weather over years. Weather makes you carry an umbrella; climate makes a place dry or wet overall.

image.alt: What is Weather? — Weather and Climate

slides.title: The Water Cycle - Rain's Journey
slides.storyContext: Grandpa Hari traces the path of water: 'Evaporation lifts water into the sky. Condensation makes clouds. Precipitation brings rain back to Earth.'

points.label: Evaporation
points.text: Heat from the sun turns water (oceans, rivers, lakes, soil) into invisible water vapor. The vapor rises into the sky.

points.label: Condensation
points.text: High in the sky, it's cold. Water vapor cools down and turns back into tiny water droplets. Millions of droplets form a cloud.

points.label: Precipitation
points.text: When droplets in a cloud get heavy enough, they fall as rain (or snow in cold places, or sleet, or hail).

points.label: Collection
points.text: Rain falls into oceans, rivers, lakes, and soil. The cycle starts again.

example.problem: A puddle disappears on a sunny day even though it doesn't rain. Where does the water go?
example.solution: Heat from the sun causes evaporation. The water turns into water vapor and rises into the sky. You can't see it, but it's there heading toward the clouds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Water travels in a circle — the sun heats it to vapor (evaporation), it rises and cools to droplets (condensation), drops as rain (precipitation), and the sun heats it again.

image.alt: The Water Cycle - Rain's Journey — Weather and Climate

slides.title: Clouds - Made of Water Droplets
slides.storyContext: Ravi points at the sky. 'Different clouds mean different weather. Divya, can you tell which will rain?'

points.label: What clouds are
points.text: Clouds are billions of tiny water droplets (or ice crystals in cold air) floating together. They form when water vapor condenses high in the atmosphere.

points.label: Cloud types
points.text: Cumulus (white, puffy, fair weather), stratus (flat, gray, low), cirrus (wispy, high, icy), nimbus (dark, brings rain or thunderstorms).

points.label: Cloud height
points.text: Height affects weather. Low clouds = rain or drizzle. High clouds = fair weather. Dark clouds = heavy rain coming.

example.problem: Why are clouds white but the sky is blue?
example.solution: Water droplets scatter all colors of light equally — that looks white to us. Clear air lets blue light scatter more — that looks blue.

slides.inSimpleWords: Clouds are floating water — billions of droplets stuck together, invisible until they condense and show as white or gray shapes in the sky.

slides.title: Wind - Moving Air
slides.storyContext: A strong breeze shakes the trees. Grandpa Hari explains: 'Wind is air moving. Why does air move? Because the sun heats Earth unevenly.'

points.label: What causes wind
points.text: The sun heats land and water unevenly. Warm air over the ocean rises. Cool air over land sinks. Moving air between them = wind.

points.label: Local vs. global winds
points.text: Sea breeze (daytime, ocean to land). Land breeze (nighttime, land to ocean). Trade winds and monsoon winds are large patterns.

points.label: Monsoon
points.text: India's monsoon is a seasonal wind shift. In June-September, winds blow from the ocean and bring heavy rain. This is India's main rainy season.

example.problem: Why does it always get windy just before heavy rain arrives?
example.solution: Heavy rain clouds are pushed by strong winds. The wind speeds up as it brings the clouds closer. When clouds arrive, wind and rain come together.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wind is air on the move — the sun heats things unevenly and pushes the air around, creating breezes and storms.

slides.title: Temperature - Hot and Cold
slides.storyContext: Divya checks a thermometer every morning and evening for a month. 'Why is it hotter at noon than at sunrise? Why are nights cooler than days?'

points.label: Day and night
points.text: The sun is high in the sky at noon — lots of rays hit Earth → hot. At sunrise and sunset, sun is low — rays spread out → cool. At night, no sun → coldest.

points.label: Seasons
points.text: Earth tilts. In summer, India tilts toward the sun → very hot. In winter, India tilts away → cool. Spring and fall are in between.

points.label: Ocean effect
points.text: Coastal cities are cooler in summer (ocean absorbs heat) and warmer in winter (ocean releases heat). Inland cities are hotter in summer, colder in winter.

example.problem: India is hot in May and June. Why is it even hotter just before monsoon rain arrives?
example.solution: Summer heat builds up. Air over land and ocean gets very hot and humidity rises (lots of water vapor). Clouds form but haven't released rain yet. The air is hot and sticky.

slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature depends on the sun's angle, the season, and whether you're near water — the whole Earth is constantly tilted and spinning, so temperature changes constantly.

slides.title: Seasons in India
slides.storyContext: Grandpa Hari points at the calendar. 'See how the year divides? Each season brings different weather and affects our crops.'

points.label: Summer (March-May)
points.text: Very hot, especially in May-June. Dry winds. Temperature can reach 45°C in North India. People drink lots of water, use fans and shade.

points.label: Monsoon (June-September)
points.text: Heavy rain, winds, and cooler temperatures. The southwest monsoon brings 80% of India's yearly rainfall. Farmers plant crops now.

points.label: Fall/Autumn (October-November)
points.text: Rains decrease. Temperature drops. Clear skies. Crops mature and are harvested. Pleasant weather for outdoor work.

points.label: Winter (December-February)
points.text: Cool and dry, especially in North India (10-15°C). South India stays warmer (20-25°C). Clear skies, less rain. Winter crops grow.

example.problem: Why do farmers plant seeds just as the monsoon rains arrive?
example.solution: They know from generations of watching the sky: June rains = soil moisture → seeds can germinate and grow. Planting now means crops are ready to harvest by October-November.

slides.inSimpleWords: India has four seasons with different temperatures, rain, and winds — each season is perfect for certain crops and activities.

slides.title: Reading the Weather Like Grandpa
slides.storyContext: Grandpa Hari teaches Divya to predict weather by watching the sky, wind, and clouds — like farmers have done for thousands of years.

example.problem: Grandpa says: 'If the evening sky is red, tomorrow will be fair. If the morning sky is red, rain is coming.' Is this science or superstition?
example.solution: This is science. Red sky = dust particles in the air. Evening red = dust from today still in air = fair tomorrow. Morning red = dust from a distant storm coming = rain coming soon. Grandpa's rule works because he's observing atmospheric particles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Farmers have watched weather patterns for millennia — they read clouds, wind, temperature, and animal behavior to predict rain and seasons.

slides.title: Predict the Weather
slides.storyContext: Divya keeps a weather diary for two weeks. She notes temperature, clouds, wind, humidity, and rain. At the end, can she predict what weather is coming?

example.problem: You see dark nimbus clouds, strong winds from the west, and humidity rising. What will happen next?
example.solution: Heavy rain will arrive within hours. Clouds are full of water. Wind is bringing them closer. High humidity means lots of water vapor. These are all signs of an imminent thunderstorm.

slides.inSimpleWords: By watching temperature, clouds, wind, and humidity together, you can predict weather like a real meteorologist.

image.alt: Predict the Weather — Weather and Climate

slides.title: Earth's Air and Water Dance
slides.storyContext: Divya now understands that weather and climate are driven by the sun, water, and air in constant motion.

points.text: Weather is today's air conditions — temperature, clouds, rain, wind.
Climate is the average weather pattern of a place over years.
The water cycle moves water: evaporation (rises) → condensation (clouds) → precipitation (rain) → collection (repeats).
Clouds form when water vapor cools and condenses. Different clouds bring different weather.
Wind is air moving because the sun heats Earth unevenly. Monsoons are seasonal winds with heavy rain.
India has four distinct seasons with different temperatures, rain, and winds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Weather and climate are nature's rhythm — the sun heats, water rises, air moves, clouds form, and rain falls in an endless dance that shapes life on Earth.
